notice: RN bank batch 8: Respiratory I: asthma, COPD, pneumonia, oxygen and TB. Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026. See REVIEW-LOG.md.

questions.stem: A client in a severe asthma attack was wheezing loudly on arrival. Twenty minutes later, the nurse hears no wheezing and very faint breath sounds. The client is drowsy, and the SpO2 is 86%. How should the nurse interpret this change?

options.text: The bronchospasm is resolving
Airflow is now so limited that respiratory failure is imminent
The client is falling asleep from exhaustion after treatment
The pulse oximeter is malfunctioning

rationale.correct: Absent wheezing in severe asthma is an ominous sign; prepare for intubation.

perOption.a: Improvement would come with better air movement and oxygenation, not drowsiness and hypoxemia.
perOption.b: A 'silent chest' means too little air is moving to make wheezes; with drowsiness, it signals impending respiratory arrest.
perOption.c: Drowsiness with hypoxemia signals carbon dioxide retention, not rest.
perOption.d: The clinical picture matches the reading.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize a silent chest as impending respiratory failure.

questions.stem: A client with asthma arrives with wheezing, chest tightness and an SpO2 of 91%. Which medication should the nurse give first?

options.text: Albuterol by nebulizer
Salmeterol by inhaler
Montelukast orally
Fluticasone by inhaler

rationale.correct: Short-acting beta2 agonists such as albuterol are the rescue medication for acute bronchospasm.

perOption.a: A short-acting beta2 agonist rapidly relaxes the bronchial smooth muscle and is the first-line rescue drug.
perOption.b: Salmeterol is a long-acting maintenance drug and too slow for rescue.
perOption.c: Leukotriene modifiers are for prevention.
perOption.d: Inhaled steroids reduce inflammation over time but don't relieve acute bronchospasm.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose the rescue medication for an asthma exacerbation.

questions.stem: A client with asthma uses a peak flow meter. Today's reading is 45% of the client's personal best, and the client is short of breath. What should the client do according to the asthma action plan?

options.text: Continue usual medications and recheck tomorrow
Use the rescue inhaler and seek emergency care now
Double the dose of the inhaled steroid
Rest and avoid using the inhaler to prevent tolerance

rationale.correct: Peak flow zones: green 80-100%, yellow 50-79% (use rescue medication and follow the plan), red below 50% (emergency).

perOption.a: This is the green-zone response (80% or more).
perOption.b: Below 50% of personal best is the red zone and needs immediate treatment and emergency care.
perOption.c: Doubling the steroid isn't an emergency treatment.
perOption.d: Withholding rescue medication is dangerous.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client newly diagnosed with asthma. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Identify and avoid your triggers, such as smoke, dust and pet dander
Carry your rescue inhaler at all times
Use a spacer with your metered-dose inhaler
Use salmeterol when you have an asthma attack
Rinse your mouth after using your inhaled steroid
Stop your controller medication when you have no symptoms

rationale.correct: Asthma self-management combines trigger control, correct inhaler use and daily controllers, with a rescue inhaler always available.

perOption.a: Avoiding triggers reduces attacks.
perOption.b: Rapid access to albuterol is essential during an attack.
perOption.c: A spacer improves delivery to the lungs.
perOption.d: Salmeterol is a long-acting drug for maintenance, never for rescue.
perOption.f: Controller drugs prevent attacks and are taken daily even when well.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client has started montelukast for asthma. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll take it every evening."
"I'll take it when I start to wheeze."
"I'll tell my provider if I have mood changes or bad dreams."
"I'll keep using my albuterol inhaler for attacks."

rationale.correct: Leukotriene modifiers are for long-term control, not rescue; watch for neuropsychiatric effects.

perOption.a: Montelukast is usually taken once daily in the evening.
perOption.b: Montelukast prevents symptoms; it doesn't relieve acute bronchospasm.
perOption.c: Montelukast can cause neuropsychiatric effects that should be reported.
perOption.d: Albuterol remains the rescue drug.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with COPD exacerbation is receiving oxygen at 6 L/min by nasal cannula. The SpO2 is 98%, and the client has become increasingly drowsy. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Increase the oxygen to keep the client comfortable
Lower the oxygen to keep the SpO2 at 88% to 92% as prescribed and obtain an arterial blood gas
Stop the oxygen completely
Let the client sleep and reassess at the next routine check

rationale.correct: Many clients with COPD have a target SpO2 of 88% to 92%; excess oxygen may increase CO2 retention and drowsiness.

perOption.a: More oxygen can worsen carbon dioxide retention.
perOption.b: Excess oxygen in some clients with COPD can worsen hypercapnia; target saturations are lower and an ABG shows the CO2 level.
perOption.c: Stopping oxygen risks hypoxemia.
perOption.d: Increasing drowsiness may mean hypercapnia and needs action now.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage oxygen therapy in a client with COPD.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client with COPD to use pursed-lip breathing. What is the main purpose of this technique?

options.text: To strengthen the diaphragm
To keep the airways open longer during exhalation so trapped air can leave
To increase the respiratory rate
To loosen secretions

rationale.correct: Pursed-lip breathing prolongs exhalation and reduces air trapping.

perOption.a: Diaphragmatic breathing is a different technique.
perOption.b: Pursed lips create back-pressure that keeps small airways from collapsing, improving emptying.
perOption.c: The goal is a slower, controlled rate.
perOption.d: Huff coughing and airway clearance devices loosen secretions.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Explain the purpose of pursed-lip breathing.

questions.stem: A client with severe COPD has lost weight and becomes short of breath while eating. Which nutrition advice should the nurse give?

options.text: Eat three large meals a day
Eat small, frequent, high-calorie, high-protein meals and rest before eating
Drink plenty of fluids with each meal
Follow a low-calorie diet

rationale.correct: Breathing takes a lot of energy in COPD; small, frequent, nutrient-dense meals help prevent malnutrition.

perOption.a: Large meals push on the diaphragm and increase breathlessness.
perOption.b: Small meals reduce abdominal pressure, and extra calories meet the high energy cost of breathing.
perOption.c: Fluids with meals cause early fullness; they are better taken between meals.
perOption.d: Clients with COPD often need more calories, not fewer.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which findings are expected in a client with long-standing COPD? Select all that apply.

options.text: Barrel chest
Clubbing of the fingers
Use of accessory muscles to breathe
Prolonged expiration
Sudden, sharp chest pain on one side
Oxygen saturation of 99% on room air

rationale.correct: Chronic COPD findings: barrel chest, accessory muscle use, prolonged expiration, clubbing and lower baseline saturation.

perOption.a: Air trapping increases the chest's front-to-back diameter.
perOption.b: Chronic hypoxemia can cause clubbing.
perOption.c: Accessory muscles help move air when the diaphragm is flattened.
perOption.d: Narrowed airways slow air leaving the lungs.
perOption.e: Sudden pain on one side may mean a pneumothorax, a complication rather than an expected finding.
perOption.f: Clients with severe COPD often have lower baseline saturations.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with COPD has been prescribed tiotropium. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll use it once a day, every day."
"I'll use it when I suddenly can't breathe."
"I'll keep the powder out of my eyes."
"I may notice a dry mouth."

rationale.correct: Long-acting bronchodilators are maintenance drugs; short-acting beta2 agonists are for rescue.

perOption.a: Tiotropium is a once-daily maintenance drug.
perOption.b: Tiotropium is a long-acting anticholinergic for maintenance, not rescue.
perOption.c: Contact with the eyes can cause blurred vision and raise eye pressure.
perOption.d: Dry mouth is a common anticholinergic effect.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old client is admitted with suspected pneumonia. Which finding is often the earliest or only sign of pneumonia in older adults?

options.text: High fever with shaking chills
New confusion
Productive cough with rust-colored sputum
Pleuritic chest pain

rationale.correct: Older adults often show atypical signs of infection, such as confusion, falls or reduced appetite.

perOption.a: Older adults often have a blunted fever response.
perOption.b: Acute confusion or delirium is often the first sign of infection in older adults.
perOption.c: Classic signs may be absent in older adults.
perOption.d: This may be absent or not reported.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize atypical presentations of pneumonia in older adults.

questions.stem: A client has pneumonia in the right lung only. Which position will best improve oxygenation?

options.text: Lying on the right side
Lying on the left side
Prone
Supine and flat

rationale.correct: 'Good lung down' matches blood flow to ventilation in one-sided lung disease.

perOption.a: The affected lung would get more blood flow but can't oxygenate it well.
perOption.b: With the good lung down, gravity sends more blood to the lung that ventilates best.
perOption.c: Prone positioning is used for ARDS, not one-sided pneumonia.
perOption.d: A flat position reduces lung expansion.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Position a client with one-sided pneumonia to improve oxygenation.

questions.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include for a client with pneumonia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Encourage use of the incentive spirometer about 10 times an hour while awake
Encourage fluid intake of 2 to 3 L a day unless restricted
Help the client walk as tolerated
Keep the head of the bed elevated
Restrict fluids to dry up secretions
Discourage coughing to save energy

rationale.correct: Pneumonia care: airway clearance, fluids, deep breathing, mobility and positioning.

perOption.a: Deep breathing opens collapsed alveoli and helps clear secretions.
perOption.b: Fluids thin secretions.
perOption.c: Walking improves ventilation and mobilizes secretions.
perOption.d: Elevation improves lung expansion.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan care for a client with pneumonia.

questions.stem: A client with dysphagia after a stroke has been cleared for a soft diet. Which action best reduces the risk of aspiration?

options.text: Have the client lie at 30 degrees while eating
Have the client sit upright at 90 degrees and tuck the chin when swallowing
Give thin liquids with every bite
Use a straw for all liquids

rationale.correct: Aspiration precautions: upright at 90 degrees, chin tuck, small bites, thickened liquids as ordered and staying upright after meals.

perOption.a: A semi-reclined position raises aspiration risk.
perOption.b: Upright positioning and the chin tuck protect the airway.
perOption.c: Thin liquids are harder to control and more likely to be aspirated.
perOption.d: Straws can deliver liquid too quickly.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prevent aspiration in a client with dysphagia.

questions.stem: A client with COPD needs a precise, controlled concentration of oxygen. Which device should the nurse expect to use?

options.text: Nasal cannula
Venturi mask
Simple face mask
Nonrebreather mask

rationale.correct: The Venturi mask is the most precise low-flow device and is useful for clients with COPD.

perOption.a: The FiO2 from a nasal cannula varies with the breathing pattern.
perOption.b: A Venturi mask delivers a precise FiO2 (about 24% to 60%).
perOption.c: A simple mask delivers a variable FiO2.
perOption.d: A nonrebreather gives a high, imprecise FiO2.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose an oxygen device that delivers a precise FiO2.

questions.stem: A client is receiving oxygen by nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min. Which observation requires the nurse's action?

options.text: The reservoir bag collapses completely when the client breathes in
The one-way valves on the mask are in place
The mask fits snugly over the nose and mouth
SpO2 is 95%

rationale.correct: A nonrebreather's reservoir bag must stay inflated; increase the flow or check the device if it collapses.

perOption.a: The bag should stay at least partly inflated; collapse means the client isn't getting enough oxygen.
perOption.b: The valves prevent rebreathing exhaled air.
perOption.c: A snug fit is correct.
perOption.d: This is a good saturation.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A provider prescribes oxygen at 10 L/min by nasal cannula. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Set the flow at 10 L/min
Clarify the prescription with the provider
Apply a nonrebreather mask instead
Set it at 6 L/min without telling the provider

rationale.correct: A standard nasal cannula delivers 1 to 6 L/min (about 24% to 44% FiO2); higher needs call for another device, such as a high-flow cannula.

perOption.a: Nasal cannulas are generally limited to about 6 L/min (standard devices).
perOption.b: Flows above 6 L/min by standard nasal cannula dry the mucosa without increasing FiO2 much; another device is needed.
perOption.c: The nurse can't change the device without an order.
perOption.d: Changing the dose without an order isn't appropriate.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the limits of a standard nasal cannula.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the flowsheet of a client being treated for pneumonia. Highlight the findings that require follow-up.

rationale.correct: Watch for signs of deterioration: rising respiratory rate, falling saturation and changes in mental status.

perOption.r1: A falling temperature shows treatment response.
perOption.r2: Tachypnea above about 24 to 28/min is a sign of worsening respiratory status.
perOption.r4: This is expected with bacterial pneumonia.
perOption.r5: New confusion may mean worsening hypoxemia or sepsis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: How should the nurse position a client for a thoracentesis?

options.text: Sitting on the edge of the bed, leaning forward over the bedside table
Supine and flat
Trendelenburg
Prone with the arms at the sides

rationale.correct: Thoracentesis: sit upright, leaning forward. Afterward, watch for pneumothorax and bleeding.

perOption.a: This widens the spaces between the ribs and lets fluid collect at the base of the lungs.
perOption.b: This doesn't give access to the posterior chest.
perOption.c: This is unsafe and doesn't help access.
perOption.d: This doesn't spread the ribs.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client has just returned from a bronchoscopy. Which action should the nurse take before giving the client anything to drink?

options.text: Check that the gag reflex has returned
Check the client's blood glucose
Give a sip of ice water to test swallowing
Have the client lie flat for 4 hours

rationale.correct: After bronchoscopy, keep the client NPO until the gag reflex returns, usually in 2 hours.

perOption.a: The throat is numbed during the procedure; drinking before the gag reflex returns risks aspiration.
perOption.b: This isn't specific to bronchoscopy.
perOption.c: Fluids aren't given until the gag reflex is confirmed.
perOption.d: Semi-Fowler's is preferred.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client taking isoniazid for tuberculosis calls the clinic. Which report should the nurse address first?

options.text: Orange-red urine
Yellowing of the skin and dark urine
Mild nausea after taking the medication
Asking whether to take vitamin B6

rationale.correct: Isoniazid can cause hepatitis and peripheral neuropathy. Avoid alcohol, monitor liver function and give vitamin B6.

perOption.a: Orange body fluids are expected with rifampin, not a toxicity.
perOption.b: Jaundice signals hepatotoxicity, a serious adverse effect of isoniazid.
perOption.c: Mild nausea can be managed.
perOption.d: Pyridoxine is often prescribed to prevent neuropathy; this is a teaching question.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is starting treatment for active pulmonary tuberculosis. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll take my medications for at least 6 months."
"I'll stop the medications once my cough goes away."
"I'll cover my mouth and nose when I cough."
"I'll need sputum tests to show I'm no longer contagious."

rationale.correct: TB treatment needs months of adherence, often with directly observed therapy, to cure it and prevent resistance.

perOption.a: Treatment usually lasts 6 to 9 months.
perOption.b: Stopping early leads to relapse and drug resistance.
perOption.c: This reduces transmission.
perOption.d: Negative sputum tests guide when isolation ends.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client to use an incentive spirometer. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Hold the breath for 3 to 5 seconds, then breathe out slowly
Seal the lips around the mouthpiece
Breathe in slowly and deeply, raising the indicator

rationale.correct: Incentive spirometry: sit up, exhale, seal, inhale slowly and deeply, hold, exhale. Repeat about 10 times an hour while awake.

perOption.a: Sitting upright allows full lung expansion.
perOption.b: This empties the lungs before the deep breath.
perOption.c: A tight seal measures the breath accurately.
perOption.d: Slow, deep breaths open collapsed alveoli.
perOption.e: Holding the breath keeps the alveoli open longer.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client has had influenza symptoms for 24 hours and is prescribed oseltamivir. What should the nurse tell the client about this medication?

options.text: "It works best when started within 48 hours of the first symptoms."
"It replaces your yearly flu vaccine."
"It kills the bacteria that cause the flu."
"You'll only need one dose."

rationale.correct: Start influenza antivirals within 48 hours of symptom onset; vaccination is still recommended every year.

perOption.a: Antivirals reduce the length and severity of illness most when started early.
perOption.b: Oseltamivir doesn't replace vaccination.
perOption.c: Influenza is a virus.
perOption.d: Treatment is usually twice daily for 5 days.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.
